item.title: Cluster / Instance
item.description:
Select instance and cluster types that meet your requirements.

Pigsty supports several PostgreSQL instance and cluster types:

  • Primary: Define a single instance cluster.
  • Replica: Define a basic HA cluster with one primary and one replica.
  • Offline: Define an instance dedicated to OLAP/ETL/interactive queries
  • Sync Standby: Enable synchronous commit to ensure no data loss.
  • Quorum Commit: Use quorum sync commit for a higher consistency level.
  • Standby Cluster: Clone an existing cluster and follow it
  • Delayed Cluster: Clone an existing cluster for emergency data recovery
  • Citus Cluster: Define a Citus distributed database cluster

item.title: Parameter Optimization Policy
item.description:
Pigsty provides four parameter templates for different workloads. Select a template with pg_conf.

  • tiny.yml: Optimized for small nodes, VMs, and demos (the template is labeled for 1-3 cores)
  • oltp.yml: Optimized for OLTP workloads and latency-sensitive applications (4C8GB+) (default template)
  • olap.yml: Optimized for OLAP workloads and throughput (4C8G+)
  • crit.yml: Optimized for data consistency and critical applications (4C8G+)

The following sections describe the optimization settings for these four templates.

Memory Parameter Tuning

Pigsty detects the system’s memory size. It uses this value to set the maximum number of connections and memory-related parameters.

item.title: RPO Trade-offs
item.description:
RPO (Recovery Point Objective) defines the maximum amount of data loss allowed when the primary fails.

Critical data, such as financial transactions, typically requires RPO = 0: no data loss.

Stricter RPO targets increase write latency and reduce throughput. Replica failure can also make the primary unavailable. Some workloads accept limited data loss for higher performance and availability.

Trade-offs

Asynchronous replicas normally lag behind the primary by about 10KB–100KB or 100µs–10ms, depending on network and throughput. At primary failure, a replica might not have received the latest data. Promotion can lose those unreplicated changes.

item.title: Kernel Version
item.description:
Choosing a “kernel” in Pigsty means determining the PostgreSQL major version, mode/distribution, packages to install, and tuning templates to load.

The Pigsty v4.5 source supports PostgreSQL 14-18 and uses 18 by default. Use the following configuration settings to select a kernel.

Major Version and Packages

  • pg_version: Select the PostgreSQL major version. The default is 18. Pigsty maps the version to the correct package name prefix.
  • pg_packages: Select core packages with package aliases. The default, pgsql-main pgsql-common, includes the kernel, Patroni, PgBouncer, pgBackRest, and other common tools.
  • pg_extensions: Select additional extension packages. Aliases are supported. The default is empty, which installs only core dependencies.
all:
 vars:
 pg_version: 18
 pg_packages: [ pgsql-main, pgsql-common ]
 pg_extensions: [ postgis, timescaledb, pgvector, pgml ]

During installation, Ansible downloads packages for pg_version=18 and installs extension files on the system. Database initialization scripts can then run CREATE EXTENSION.

item.title: OLTP Template
item.description:
oltp.yml is Pigsty’s default configuration template for online transaction processing (OLTP). It is designed for CPUs with 4-128 cores and provides high concurrency, low latency, and high throughput.

Pair with node_tune = oltp for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the OLTP template for:

  • E-commerce: Order processing, inventory, user transactions
  • Social apps: User feeds, messaging, following relationships
  • Gaming backends: Player data, leaderboards, game state
  • SaaS applications: Multi-tenant business systems
  • Web apps: CRUD-intensive workloads

item.title: E-R Model of PostgreSQL Cluster
item.description:
PGSQL organizes PostgreSQL as clusters. Each cluster is a logical group of database instances connected through primary-replica relationships.

Each cluster is an autonomous business unit with at least one primary instance. It exposes database capabilities through services.

There are four core entities in Pigsty’s PGSQL module:

  • Cluster: An autonomous PostgreSQL business unit and the top-level namespace for other entities.
  • Service: A named abstraction that exposes capabilities and routes traffic through node ports.
  • Instance: One PostgreSQL server, including its running processes and database files, on one node.
  • Node: A hardware resource that runs Linux and Systemd. It can be a physical server, VM, container, or Pod.

Two business entities, Database and Role, complete this logical model:

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Users
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages users declaratively. First define users in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-user <cls> <username> to create or modify them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_users: [{ name: dbuser_app, password: 'DBUser.App', pgbouncer: true }] # <--- Define user list here!
Script
bin/pgsql-user <cls> <username> # Create/modify <username> user on <cls> cluster
Playbook
./pgsql-user.yml -l pg-meta -e username=dbuser_app # Use playbook to create/modify user
Example
bin/pgsql-user pg-meta dbuser_app # Create/modify dbuser_app user on pg-meta cluster

For the complete user definition reference, see User Configuration. See Access Control for roles and privileges, and Authentication for credential management.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Databases
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages databases declaratively. First define databases in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-db <cls> <dbname> to create or modify them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_databases: [{ name: some_db }]  # <--- Define database list here!
Script
bin/pgsql-db <cls> <dbname> # Create/modify <dbname> database on <cls> cluster
Playbook
./pgsql-db.yml -l pg-meta -e dbname=some_db # Use playbook to create/modify database
Example
bin/pgsql-db pg-meta some_db # Create/modify some_db database on pg-meta cluster

For the complete database definition reference, see Database Configuration. For database access permissions, see Access Control: Database Isolation.

item.title: Failure Model
item.description:
Patroni failures have 10 categories by failure target. Detection paths group them into five categories, described here.

# Failure Scenario Description Final Path
1 PG process crash crash, OOM killed Active Detection
2 PG connection refused max_connections Active Detection
3 PG zombie Process alive but unresponsive Active Detection (timeout)
4 Patroni process crash kill -9, OOM Passive Detection
5 Patroni zombie Process alive but stuck Watchdog
6 Node down Power outage, hardware failure Passive Detection
7 Node zombie IO hang, CPU starvation Watchdog
8 Primary ↔ DCS network failure Firewall, switch failure Network Partition
9 Storage failure Disk failure, disk full, mount failure Active Detection or Watchdog
10 Manual switchover Switchover/Failover Manual Trigger

For RTO calculations, all failures follow two paths. This section calculates their minimum, maximum, and average recovery times.

item.title: OLAP Template
item.description:
olap.yml is optimized for online analytical processing (OLAP) on CPUs with 4-128 cores. It supports large queries, high parallelism, relaxed timeouts, and aggressive vacuum.

Pair with node_tune = olap for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the OLAP template for:

  • Data warehouses: Historical data storage, multidimensional analysis
  • BI reports: Complex report queries, dashboard data sources
  • ETL processing: Data extraction, transformation, loading
  • Data analysis: Ad-hoc queries, data exploration
  • HTAP mixed workloads: Analytical replicas

item.title: Package Alias
item.description:
PostgreSQL package names differ between operating systems:

  • EL systems (RHEL/Rocky/Alma/…) use formats like pgvector_18, postgis36_18*
  • Debian/Ubuntu systems use formats like postgresql-18-pgvector, postgresql-18-postgis-3

Without aliases, you need different naming rules for each system. You must also include the correct PostgreSQL version in the names.

Package Alias

item.title: CRIT Template
item.description:
crit.yml is for transactional workloads with increased consistency and audit requirements. It forces data checksums and Patroni strict synchronous mode. It also adds connection logging and adjusts selected WAL, timeout, and parallel-query parameters.

The template increases write latency and may block writes when no synchronous replica is available. Before use, confirm consistency objectives, failure domains, client commit settings, and availability requirements.

Also evaluate node_tune: crit. You can select host tuning and database parameters independently.

item.title: Patroni HA Management
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty uses Patroni to manage PostgreSQL clusters. It handles configuration changes, status checks, switchovers, restarts, replica reinitialization, and other operations.

To manage clusters with Patroni, use one of these identities:

  • On an INFRA node, use an administration user to manage all clusters in the environment.
  • On a PGSQL node, use pg_dbsu, which defaults to postgres, to manage only the current cluster.

Patroni provides the patronictl administration CLI. Pigsty provides the pg wrapper alias to simplify its use.

item.title: User/Role
item.description:
In this document, “user” refers to a logical object within a database cluster created with CREATE USER/ROLE.

In PostgreSQL, users belong to the database cluster, rather than a specific database. Create business users before you create business databases.

Pigsty defines roles and users through two config parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: Define globally shared roles and users
  • pg_users: Define business users and roles at cluster level

The first parameter defines roles and users shared across the environment. The second defines business roles and users for one cluster. Both parameters use arrays of user definition objects. Pigsty creates users and roles in array order. Thus, a later user can belong to an earlier role.

item.title: Database
item.description:
In this document, “database” refers to a logical object within a database cluster created with CREATE DATABASE.

A PostgreSQL cluster can serve multiple databases at the same time. Define the required databases in the Pigsty cluster configuration.

Pigsty customizes the template1 database with default schemas, extensions, and privileges. New databases inherit these settings from template1. Use template to select another template for instant database cloning.

By default, Pigsty adds each application database to the PgBouncer connection pool with a 1:1 mapping. pg_exporter discovers application databases automatically to monitor their objects. Pigsty also registers all databases as PostgreSQL data sources in Grafana on every INFRA node for PGCAT dashboards.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL HBA Rules
item.description:
Quick Start

Pigsty manages HBA rules declaratively. First define HBA rules in the inventory. Then run bin/pgsql-hba <cls> to refresh them.

pg-meta:
 hosts: { 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary } }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_hba_rules: # <--- Define HBA rules here!
 - {user: dbuser_app, db: app, addr: intra, auth: pwd, title: 'app access'}
 - {user: dbuser_api, db: all, addr: world, auth: ssl, title: 'api ssl access'}
Script
bin/pgsql-hba <cls> # Refresh PostgreSQL and Pgbouncer HBA rules for cluster
bin/pgsql-hba <cls> <ip>... # Refresh HBA rules for specific instances
Playbook
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pg_hba,pg_reload # Refresh PostgreSQL HBA only
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pgbouncer_hba,pgbouncer_reload # Refresh Pgbouncer HBA only
./pgsql.yml -l <cls> -t pg_hba,pg_reload,pgbouncer_hba,pgbouncer_reload # Refresh both
Example
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta # Refresh pg-meta cluster HBA rules
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta 10.10.10.10 # Refresh specific instance only
bin/pgsql-hba pg-meta 10.10.10.11 10.10.10.12 # Refresh multiple instances

For rule syntax, see HBA Configuration. For authentication methods, default boundaries, and credential management, see Authentication.

item.title: Pgbouncer Connection Pooling
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty uses Pgbouncer for PostgreSQL connection pooling. By default, it listens on port 6432 and proxies connections to local PostgreSQL on port 5432.

This component is optional. If you do not need many connections, transaction pooling, or query metrics, you can disable it. You can also connect directly to the database or leave Pgbouncer unused.

User & Database Management

Pigsty automatically manages Pgbouncer users and databases. When you create databases or users, it applies the database configuration and user configuration.

item.title: TINY Template
item.description:
tiny.yml is optimized for micro instances and environments with limited resources. It is designed for CPUs with 1-3 cores. It minimizes resource use, limits memory allocation, and disables parallel queries.

Pair with node_tune = tiny for OS-level tuning.

Use Cases

Use the TINY template for:

  • Dev/test: Local development, CI/CD testing
  • Low-spec VMs: 1-2 core CPU, 1-4GB RAM cloud instances
  • Edge computing: Raspberry Pi, embedded devices
  • Demos: Quick Pigsty experience
  • Personal projects: Resource-limited blogs, small apps

Resource constraints:

item.title: HBA Rules
item.description:
Overview

HBA (Host-Based Authentication) controls who can connect to a database, from which source, and with which authentication method. For the authentication model and default rules, see Authentication. Pigsty manages HBA rules through pg_default_hba_rules and pg_hba_rules.

Pigsty generates these files during cluster initialization or HBA refresh:

Config File Path Description
PostgreSQL HBA /pg/data/pg_hba.conf PostgreSQL server HBA rules
PgBouncer HBA /etc/pgbouncer/pgb_hba.conf Connection pool HBA rules

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Access control combines roles, object privileges, database ACLs, and HBA. This page describes configuration parameters. For design and boundaries, see Access Control Concepts.

Pigsty provides a compact ACL model described by these parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: system roles and system users.
  • pg_users: application users and roles.
  • pg_default_privileges: default privileges on objects created by managed administrators and owners.
  • pg_revoke_public, pg_default_schemas, and pg_default_extensions: default behavior for template1.

Manage these parameters together with HBA and database definitions to produce reproducible access-control configuration.

item.title: Managing PostgreSQL Component Services
item.description:
Overview

The Pigsty PGSQL module has multiple components. Each component runs as a systemd service on nodes, except pgBackRest.

To maintain production PostgreSQL clusters, learn how these components work and how to manage them.

Component Port Service Name Description
Patroni 8008 patroni HA manager, manages PostgreSQL lifecycle
PostgreSQL 5432 postgres Placeholder service, not used, for emergency
Pgbouncer 6432 pgbouncer Connection pooling middleware, traffic entry
PgBackRest - - pgBackRest has no daemon service
HAProxy 543x haproxy Load balancer, exposes database services
pg_exporter 9630 pg_exporter PostgreSQL metrics exporter
pgbouncer_exporter 9631 pgbouncer_exporter Pgbouncer metrics exporter
vip-manager - vip-manager Optional, manages L2 VIP address floating
Important

Do not manage the PostgreSQL service directly with systemctl. Patroni manages PostgreSQL. Use patronictl commands. Direct PostgreSQL operations can make Patroni state inconsistent and trigger an unexpected failover. Use the postgres service only for emergencies when Patroni fails.

item.title: Parameters
item.description:
You can set PostgreSQL parameters at several levels with different scopes and priorities. Pigsty supports four levels, from global to local:

Level Scope Configuration Method Storage Location
Cluster All instances in cluster Patroni DCS / Tuning Templates etcd + postgresql.conf
Instance Single PG instance pg_parameters / ALTER SYSTEM postgresql.auto.conf
Database All sessions in a DB pg_databases[].parameters pg_db_role_setting
User All sessions of a user pg_users[].parameters pg_db_role_setting

Priority from low to high: Cluster < Instance < Database < User < Session (SET command). Higher priority settings override lower ones.

item.title: Upgrading PostgreSQL Major/Minor Versions
item.description:
Quick Start

PostgreSQL has two types of version upgrade: minor and major. Their risk and complexity differ substantially.

Type Example Downtime Data Compatibility Risk
Minor upgrade 17.2 → 17.3 Seconds (rolling) Fully compatible Low
Major upgrade 17 → 18 Minutes Requires data dir upgrade Medium
Minor

ansible <cls> -b -a 'yum upgrade -y postgresql17*'
pg restart --role replica --force <cls>
pg switchover <cls>
pg restart <cls> <old-primary> --force

bin/pgsql-add pg-new # Create new version cluster
# Configure logical replication to sync data...
# Switch traffic to new cluster
Extension
ansible <cls> -b -a 'yum upgrade -y postgis36_17*'
psql -c 'ALTER EXTENSION postgis UPDATE;'

item.title: High Availability
item.description:
Overview

Pigsty PostgreSQL clusters include HA through Patroni, Etcd, and HAProxy.

A cluster with two or more instances gains automatic HA without extra configuration. A surviving instance can provide the complete database service. Clients can connect through any cluster node without tracking primary-replica changes.

Default norm mode targets RTO below 45 seconds. With asynchronous replication, pg_rpo=1MiB limits sampled lag for failover candidates. It does not bound actual data loss. Strict synchronous mode with crit.yml gives acknowledged transactions RPO = 0 during failover. Configure these settings for your hardware and reliability requirements.

PGSQL organizes PostgreSQL as clusters. Each cluster is a logical group of database instances connected through primary-replica relationships.

item.title: Point-in-Time Recovery — A Time Machine for PostgreSQL
item.description:
Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) can restore an earlier cluster state after accidental deletion of data, a table, or a database.

Pigsty enables PITR in its standard PostgreSQL configuration. This work once required specialist DBA knowledge.

Replication Is Not Backup

High availability can fail over to another instance after hardware failure. However, replication is not backup.

Streaming replication sends every primary change to replicas within milliseconds. This includes DELETE without WHERE or DROP TABLE against the wrong database. Failover handles machine failure. If the data is wrong, every replica can contain the same error.

item.title: RTO Trade-offs
item.description:
RTO (Recovery Time Objective) defines the maximum time required for the system to restore write capability when the primary fails.

Critical transaction systems typically need the shortest practical RTO, often below one minute.

Shorter RTO increases false failover risk. Network jitter can appear to be a failure. Cross-datacenter or cross-region deployments often allow 1–2 minutes to reduce this risk.

Trade-offs

pg_rto controls the failover unavailability limit. Presets fast, norm, safe, and wide support different network and deployment conditions. The default is norm, approximately 45 seconds.

item.title: How PITR Works
item.description:
A database is a state machine. WAL (Write-Ahead Log) records its changes in order. PostgreSQL writes each change to WAL before applying it to data files. Keep a physical snapshot and all later WAL to replay the database to a selected consistent state.

PITR combines three elements: a snapshot (base backup), history (WAL archive), and a target where replay stops.

Snapshot: Base Backup

A base backup is a physical snapshot of the whole PostgreSQL cluster. It provides the recovery starting point. Pigsty uses pgBackRest to manage three backup types:

item.title: PITR Architecture
item.description:
The PITR principle is simple, but implementation must address several constraints. WAL archiving must not block production writes. Object storage backups need encryption. Backup jobs must follow the primary after failover, and shared repositories must isolate clusters. Large numbers of small objects can also limit throughput.

Pigsty uses pgBackRest with production defaults that address these constraints. This page describes the engine, repository abstraction, archive path, scheduler, and execution on the current primary.

item.title: PITR Tradeoffs
item.description:
Backups require storage, network traffic, and operational work. They determine how much data you can recover and how quickly service returns. More history usually requires more capacity. A shorter RTO usually requires newer backups and tested procedures.

A backup policy must define repository location, history retention, and backup frequency.

Where: Choose the Failure Domain

Repository location is the most important choice. It determines which disasters the backup can survive.

item.title: Declarative Recovery
item.description:
A backup must support recovery when an incident occurs. Traditional PITR requires connected manual steps: pause HA, stop PostgreSQL, prepare recovery settings, restore the backup, and replay WAL. Then validate the target, rebuild metadata, and start the cluster again.

Pigsty uses declarative configuration for recovery. Declare the recovery target. The tools stop the cluster, restore data, replay WAL, and return control to the operator.

Declare a Recovery Target

Set pg_pitr to describe the target. Run pgsql-pitr.yml to restore it. The most common form selects a specific time:

item.title: PITR Scenarios
item.description:
Decisions can consume much of the available incident response time. Pigsty automates recovery steps, but the operator must decide three things. Select the target, choose in-place or clone recovery, and define how to validate the result.

Read and rehearse this framework before an incident.

Decision Framework

Scenario Typical problem Recommended workflow Target
Accidental DML DELETE or UPDATE affects the wrong rows Clone, validate, then copy back data time / xid
Dropped table, schema, or database DROP or an incorrect migration Clone, validate, then copy back objects time / name
Defective release or batch corruption Software writes incorrect data for a period Clone and compare before choosing repair or cutover time / xid
Audit, investigation, or forensics Inspect historical state Clone and hold at the target for inspection time / lsn
Whole-cluster or site loss Hosts or storage are gone or encrypted Recover in place on replacement infrastructure default / time

Two principles apply throughout:

item.title: Service Access
item.description:
Split read and write operations, route traffic correctly, and deliver PostgreSQL cluster capabilities reliably.

A service exposes database cluster capabilities through a stable interface that hides the underlying cluster details.

Services provide stable production access, especially during HA failover. Personal users usually do not need this abstraction.

Personal Users

Services are mainly for production. Personal users with one node can connect directly through the instance name or IP address.

item.title: Security and Compliance
item.description:
Databases usually store the most valuable and sensitive data in an information system. Attacks and failures can therefore have severe consequences. Security requires multiple controls: who can connect, what they can do, and whether traffic is protected. It must also record operations and support recovery of damaged, lost, or deleted data.

Pigsty provides a default security baseline through declarative configuration. Declare HBA rules, roles and privileges, certificates, encryption, backups, and audit policies as parameters in the inventory. Idempotent playbooks render and apply these settings.

item.title: Security Model
item.description:
Identify the root of trust and defensive layers before selecting security features. The root of trust needs the strongest protection. Multiple layers preserve some protection if one fails.

Trust Boundaries

Pigsty uses Ansible for declarative deployment. Its administration node is the control plane and needs the strongest protection.

Role Assets and Privileges
Admin node The pigsty.yml inventory, which normally contains system and application credentials; the CA private key; SSH administration access to every node
INFRA nodes Monitoring and alerts, DNS, Nginx ingress, and software repositories
Database nodes Database instances, local dbsu, and restricted sudo
Clients Database credentials or client certificates; access through service ports, HBA, and authentication

These roles have different capabilities, not a simple hierarchy. Protect these three assets in particular:

item.title: Authentication
item.description:
pg_hba.conf defines PostgreSQL Host-Based Authentication. It controls who can connect, the source address, the database, and the required identity check.

Manual HBA maintenance across a cluster requires care. Primary and replica rules can differ, and each instance stores its configuration in its data directory. Without a shared declaration and refresh process, instance rules can diverge.

Pigsty declares HBA rules in the inventory through declarative configuration. Playbooks render and distribute them consistently.

item.title: Access Control
item.description:
Authentication verifies identity. Authorization determines what that identity can do.

PostgreSQL GRANT and REVOKE provide precise control. Privilege problems usually arise from missing default conventions. Examples include making an application account the owner, retaining temporary superuser access after troubleshooting, and omitting grants on new tables.

Pigsty provides four role tiers, default privileges, and database isolation. This starting model reduces manual grants per database. Operators must still assign roles to match business boundaries and regularly review effective privileges.

item.title: Encrypted Communication
item.description:
TLS can provide transport encryption, server authentication, and client authentication. Configure each protection separately. Enabling server TLS does not make clients verify the server or make the server require client certificates.

Most TLS operational work involves certificate issuance, distribution, trust, and rotation. Without central management, services often skip verification or keep plaintext connections.

Pigsty manages PKI declaratively. Deployment creates a local self-signed CA, issues component certificates, and distributes trust. TLS is then ready for use.

item.title: Data Security
item.description:
Network boundaries, authentication, and access control reduce incident risk. Data controls must limit damage and support recovery after hardware failure, leaked credentials, or operator errors.

Data security must provide integrity, recoverability, confidentiality if copied, and records of what happened.

Integrity

Bad disk sectors, memory bit flips, and firmware defects can cause silent data corruption, with no immediate error. Pigsty enables pg_checksum: true by default. Initialization uses data-checksums. PostgreSQL calculates each page checksum on write and checks it on read.

item.title: Compliance
item.description:
Compliance requires continuous evidence of three elements:

  • Configuration: Security controls must be enabled. Pigsty directly provides configuration.
  • Process: The organization must establish access approval, change management, recovery exercises, and related procedures.
  • Evidence: Records must show that configuration and processes remain effective. The inventory, runtime logs, and monitoring system provide part of this evidence.

This page provides a pre-launch checklist and maps Pigsty capabilities to common compliance frameworks. These mappings support architecture and gap analysis. They are not an MLPS assessment, SOC 2 audit opinion, or legal advice.

item.title: Getting Started with PostgreSQL
item.description:
PostgreSQL is an open-source relational database. It can store and retrieve different types of data. This guide uses PG as an abbreviation for PostgreSQL.

Use this guide if you know basic Linux commands and want to start with PostgreSQL in Pigsty. The examples use the default single-node installation. For production clusters with multiple nodes, see Service Access.

Basics

The default single-node template creates the pg-meta cluster on the current node. This cluster has one primary instance. PostgreSQL listens on port 5432. The template also creates the meta database.

item.title: PostgreSQL Mongo Mode
item.description:
The mongo configuration template is a PostgreSQL deployment mode, not an independent Pigsty module. It combines:

  • PostgreSQL 18 managed by the standard PGSQL module
  • The documentdb extension and its required preload libraries
  • A stateless FerretDB proxy deployed with Pigsty’s Docker APP workflow

PostgreSQL manages all data, high availability, backups, monitoring, and the database lifecycle. FerretDB provides only the MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint.

Quick Start

The default template is a single-node deployment on 10.10.10.10. FerretDB listens on loopback by default.

item.title: Configuration
item.description:
Pigsty uses configuration to control PostgreSQL behavior. This configuration combines inventory files in ~/pigsty/conf/*.yml with PGSQL parameters. After you write the configuration, you can reproduce a customized cluster in a few minutes. The configuration includes instances, users, databases, access control, extensions, and tuning policies.

Configuration Entry

  1. Prepare Inventory: Copy a pigsty/conf/*.yml template or write an Ansible inventory. Put cluster groups (all.children.<cls>.hosts) and global variables (all.vars) in the same file.
  2. Define Parameters: Override the required PGSQL parameters in vars. The override order is global → cluster → host. The last applicable setting determines the value.
  3. Apply Configuration: Use ./configure -c <conf>, bin/pgsql-add <cls>, and other playbooks to apply the configuration. Pigsty generates the required Patroni, PgBouncer, and pgBackRest files from these parameters.

The default demonstration inventory, conf/pgsql.yml, provides a minimal example. It defines one pg-meta cluster, global pg_version: 18, and a few application users and databases. You can add more clusters to this configuration.

item.title: PostgreSQL Security
item.description:
PostgreSQL security combines authentication, authorization, network boundaries, encrypted communication, data protection, and operating procedures. Pigsty provides configuration parameters for these mechanisms. Operators must still harden, verify, and audit the deployment for its environment.

Concepts and Boundaries

  • Access Control Configuration: configure default roles, application users, object privileges, and database ACLs.
  • User Configuration: define user attributes, role membership, and connection-pool options.
  • CRIT Parameter Template: critical parameters for synchronous replication, checksums, logging, and watchdog.

item.title: User / Role
item.description:
In this context, users refer to logical objects within a database cluster created using the SQL commands CREATE USER/ROLE.

In PostgreSQL, users belong to the database cluster, rather than a specific database. Create business users before you create business databases.

Defining Users

Pigsty defines roles and users in database clusters through two configuration parameters:

  • pg_default_roles: Defines globally unified roles and users
  • pg_users: Defines business users and roles at the database cluster level

The first parameter defines roles and users shared across the environment. The second defines business roles and users for individual clusters. Both use arrays of user definition objects.

item.title: Database
item.description:
In this context, Database refers to the logical object created using the SQL command CREATE DATABASE within a database cluster.

A PostgreSQL server can serve multiple databases at the same time. In Pigsty, define the required databases in the cluster configuration.

Pigsty customizes the default template database, template1. It creates default schemas, installs default extensions, and configures default privileges. New databases inherit these settings from template1 by default.

By default, Pigsty adds each business database to the Pgbouncer connection pool with a 1:1 mapping. pg_exporter automatically discovers all business databases and monitors their objects.

item.title: Authentication / HBA
item.description:
Detailed explanation of Host-Based Authentication (HBA) in Pigsty.

Authentication supports Access Control and Default Privileges. PostgreSQL supports several authentication methods.

This page describes HBA, or Host-Based Authentication. HBA rules specify which users can access each database, from which locations, and with which authentication methods.

Client Authentication

Users must authenticate before they connect to a PostgreSQL database. By default, they use a password.

You can put the password in the connection string, but this is not secure. Alternatively, use the PGPASSWORD environment variable or a .pgpass file. For details, see psql and PostgreSQL Connection Strings.

item.title: Troubleshooting
item.description:
This document lists possible PostgreSQL and Pigsty failures. It gives standard procedures to locate, resolve, and analyze them.

Disk Space Exhausted

Disk space exhaustion is the most common type of failure.

Symptoms

If the database disk is full, PostgreSQL cannot operate normally. Logs repeatedly report “no space left on device”, and new writes fail. PostgreSQL may also report a PANIC and shut down.

If the permitted downtime is sufficient, you can use pg_dump | psql for offline migration.

item.title: Accidental Deletion
item.description:
Accidental Data Deletion

For a small accidental DELETE, consider pg_surgery or pg_dirtyread for selective recovery in place.

-- Immediately disable Auto Vacuum on this table and abort Auto Vacuum worker processes for this table
ALTER TABLE public.some_table SET (autovacuum_enabled = off, toast.autovacuum_enabled = off);

CREATE EXTENSION pg_dirtyread;
SELECT * FROM pg_dirtyread('tablename') AS t(col1 type1, col2 type2, ...);

If the deleted data has already been reclaimed by VACUUM, then use the general accidental deletion recovery process.

item.title: Playbook
item.description:
Pigsty provides playbooks for cluster provisioning, scaling, user and database management, monitoring, backup, recovery, and migration.

item.title: PostgreSQL
item.description:
PostgreSQL is a widely used open-source database.

Pigsty installs PostgreSQL 18 by default. It supports PostgreSQL 14 ~ 18 and provides 600 PG extensions.

Quick Start

Install Pigsty using the pgsql configuration template.

./configure -c pgsql # Use postgres kernel
./deploy.yml # Deploy the Pigsty core chain with native PostgreSQL

Most configuration templates use the PostgreSQL kernel by default. Examples include:

  • meta : Default, postgres with core extensions (vector, postgis, timescale)
  • rich : postgres with all extensions installed
  • slim : postgres only, no monitoring infrastructure
  • ha/full : 4-node sandbox for HA demonstration
  • pgsql : minimal postgres kernel configuration example

Configuration

The native PostgreSQL kernel requires no special configuration changes:

item.title: Bind a L2 VIP to PostgreSQL Primary with VIP-Manager
item.description:
If all cluster nodes share one L2 network, you can optionally define an L2 VIP for the PostgreSQL cluster.

The VIP uses Master-Backup mode. It always points to the node that runs the cluster primary instance.

VIP-Manager manages the VIP. It reads the Leader Key that Patroni writes to DCS (etcd) to determine whether the local node is primary.

Enable VIP

To enable VIP for a cluster, set pg_vip_enabled to true at cluster level. You can also enable it globally.

item.title: Deploy HA Citus Cluster
item.description:
Citus is a PostgreSQL extension that turns PostgreSQL into a distributed database. It scales horizontally across nodes to process large data volumes and query workloads.

Patroni v3.0+ provides native high-availability support for Citus. This simplifies Citus cluster setup. Pigsty also provides native support.

  • What is Citus
  • Patroni Citus Support

Note: Citus 13.x supports PostgreSQL 18, 17, 16, 15, and 14. Pigsty extension repo provides Citus ARM64 packages.

Citus Cluster

Pigsty natively supports Citus. The current complete configuration template is conf/ha/citus.yml.

item.title: Babelfish
item.description:
Babelfish is a PostgreSQL-based SQL Server compatibility layer, open-sourced by AWS.

Overview

Deploy Babelfish in mssql mode to add these features to PostgreSQL:

  • SQL Server wire protocol compatibility (TDS, 1433)
  • T-SQL compatibility
  • Unified integration with Pigsty capabilities (HA, backup, monitoring, IaC)

In Pigsty v4, Babelfish supports PostgreSQL 17/18. The default template uses pg_version: 17. Babelfish is part of Pigsty’s standard delivery process and supports all Linux platforms.

item.title: Percona
item.description:
Percona Postgres is a patched Postgres kernel with pg_tde (Transparent Data Encryption) extension.

From v4.4.0, Pigsty installs Percona PostgreSQL under the private prefix /usr/pgtde-$v. Version v4.5.0 keeps this layout, with /usr/pgtde-18 for PostgreSQL 18. The pgtde package alias installs both the kernel package and its contrib package. These packages include pg_tde, PostGIS, pgvector, wal2json, pg_repack, pgaudit, and pg_stat_monitor.

  • Performance Test for Percona Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)

Quick Start

Use Pigsty’s standard installation process with the pgtde configuration template.

item.title: openHalo
item.description:
OpenHalo is an open-source PostgreSQL kernel that provides MySQL wire-protocol compatibility.

openHalo is based on PostgreSQL 14.18 and provides wire-level compatibility with MySQL 5.7.32-log / 8.0. Pigsty delivers it through pg_mode: mysql and the openhalo package alias.

Pigsty supports OpenHalo deployment on all supported Linux platforms.

  • RPM build spec: github.com/pgsty/rpm/rpmbuild/specs/openhalodb.spec
  • DEB build spec: github.com/pgsty/deb/debbuild/openhalodb

Quick Start

Use Pigsty’s standard installation flow with the mysql template.

curl -fsSL https://repo.pigsty.io/get | bash; cd ~/pigsty;
./configure -c mysql # Use MySQL (openHalo) template
./deploy.yml # Install (change passwords in pigsty.yml before production use)

Cluster Config 

pg-meta:
 hosts:
 10.10.10.10: { pg_seq: 1, pg_role: primary }
 vars:
 pg_cluster: pg-meta
 pg_users:
 - {name: dbuser_meta ,password: DBUser.Meta ,pgbouncer: true ,roles: [dbrole_admin] ,comment: pigsty admin user }
 - {name: dbuser_view ,password: DBUser.Viewer ,pgbouncer: true ,roles: [dbrole_readonly] ,comment: read-only viewer for meta database }
 pg_databases:
 - {name: postgres, extensions: [ aux_mysql ]} # mysql-compatible database
 - {name: meta ,baseline: cmdb.sql ,comment: pigsty meta database ,schemas: [pigsty]}
 pg_hba_rules:
 - {user: dbuser_view , db: all ,addr: infra ,auth: pwd ,title: 'allow grafana dashboard access cmdb from infra nodes'}
 pg_crontab: [ '00 01 * * * /pg/bin/pg-backup full' ] # full backup at 1 AM daily

 # OpenHalo specific settings
 pg_mode: mysql
 pg_version: 14
 pg_packages: [ openhalo, pgsql-common ]

The OpenHalo extension aux_mysql provides functions and types for MySQL compatibility. Enable it in the postgres database for full compatibility behavior.

item.title: OrioleDB
item.description:
OrioleDB is a PostgreSQL storage engine extension. It claims to provide 4x OLTP performance and to eliminate xid wraparound and table bloat issues. It also claims to provide cloud-native storage, with data stored in S3.

Pigsty ships OrioleDB as a patched PostgreSQL kernel plus the OrioleDB extension.

You can run OrioleDB as an RDS with Pigsty. Current packages support PostgreSQL 16, 17, and 18 on supported Linux platforms. Set pg_mode to oriole to use the /usr/oriole-$v installation path. The orioledb package alias resolves to versioned kernel packages, such as orioledb-16, orioledb-17, and orioledb-18. The current Pigsty package line is OrioleDB 1.8 beta16.

item.title: Cloudberry
item.description:
Cloudberry is an open-source MPP data warehouse kernel derived from the Greenplum ecosystem. It supports large-scale parallel analytics workloads.

Overview

In Pigsty, Cloudberry uses gpsql mode and shares the same identity model, monitoring logic, and directory conventions as Greenplum / MatrixDB.

  • Kernel package: cloudberry
  • Mode identifier: pg_mode: gpsql
  • Role flag: gp_role: master | segment
  • Current repo version: Cloudberry 2.1.0
  • Current main package version: DEB 2.1.0-2PIGSTY, RPM 2.1.0-3PIGSTY
  • Default binary directory: /usr/cloudberry

Pigsty currently provides package delivery, node management, monitoring integration, access control, and configuration management for Cloudberry. For MPP cluster initialization, scale-out, rebalance, and other upstream operations, you should use the official Cloudberry tools.

item.title: AgensGraph
item.description:
AgensGraph is a property graph database kernel built on PostgreSQL. It supports openCypher queries and mixed Cypher/SQL workflows.

Overview

Pigsty integrates AgensGraph through pg_mode: agens while preserving most of the standard PostgreSQL operational model.

  • Kernel package: agensgraph
  • Mode identifier: pg_mode: agens
  • Current template version: AgensGraph 2.17.0
  • Current version string: PostgreSQL 17.10 (AgensGraph 2.17.0)
  • Built-in template: agens
  • Typical use cases: graph relationship analysis, path queries, knowledge graphs, and risk/association analysis layered onto relational data

AgensGraph uses the PostgreSQL wire protocol. Standard PostgreSQL clients, drivers, and connection pools can connect directly. AgensGraph adds graph objects, Cypher syntax, and the agtype data type to the database.

item.title: pgEdge
item.description:
pgEdge is a distributed PostgreSQL distribution for edge deployments. It uses Spock multi-master logical replication.

Overview

Pigsty integrates pgEdge through pg_mode: pgedge and delivers it through the standard PostgreSQL cluster workflow:

  • pgedge: a PG15, PG16, PG17, and PG18 compatible kernel; the template defaults to PG18
  • spock: Active-active multi-master logical replication
  • snowflake: Distributed unique sequences
  • lolor: Large object logical replication compatibility layer

The current Pigsty repository supplies the versioned kernel packages pgedge-15, pgedge-16, pgedge-17, and pgedge-18. The template defaults to pg_version: 18. The pgedge-$v kernel package includes the control files, SQL files, and shared libraries for spock, snowflake, and lolor. Thus, these extensions are no longer separate packages in pg_extensions. pgEdge supports the PostgreSQL wire protocol, so psql, JDBC/ODBC, DBeaver, and similar tools work as usual.

item.title: DocumentDB
item.description:
Microsoft maintains DocumentDB, an open-source PostgreSQL document database extension. FerretDB is a stateless protocol translation proxy built on DocumentDB. Together, they provide a MongoDB wire-compatible endpoint for a standard PostgreSQL kernel. Applications can connect directly with MongoDB drivers. FerretDB translates their requests into PostgreSQL operations.

This stack is not a standalone PostgreSQL fork. The data layer uses native PostgreSQL 16–18, which the standard PGSQL module manages. PostgreSQL provides persistence, transactions, high availability, backup, monitoring, and access control. FerretDB runs as a Pigsty Docker APP and handles only protocol translation.

item.title: Param Templates
item.description:
Pigsty provides four preset Patroni/PostgreSQL config templates optimized for different workloads:

Template CPU Cores Use Case Characteristics
/docs/pgsql/template/oltp.yml 4-128C OLTP transactions High concurrency, low latency
/docs/pgsql/template/olap.yml 4-128C OLAP analytics Large queries, high parallelism
/docs/pgsql/template/crit.yml 4-128C Consistency-first Consistency-first, detailed auditing
/docs/pgsql/template/tiny.yml 1-3C Tiny instances Resource-constrained envs

Use pg_conf to select a template. The default is /docs/pgsql/template/oltp.yml.

The database tuning template pg_conf should be paired with the OS tuning template node_tune.

All four standard templates set wal_level to logical. PostgreSQL 18.6 adds the output_plugin_libraries security allowlist. Pigsty permits the built-in pgoutput and test_decoding plugins, plus wal2json from the default pgsql-main package set. Before you use another logical-decoding output plugin, review its code and privilege boundary. Then add its exact library name through pg_parameters. Patroni filters the template setting on older PostgreSQL versions that do not support it.

item.title: PG Kernels
item.description:
In Pigsty, you can replace the native PostgreSQL kernel with a variant that provides specialized features.

Pigsty supports multiple PostgreSQL kernels and compatibility branches within one operational framework. These kernels provide compatibility layers, multi-master replication, graph queries, MPP warehousing, transparent encryption, and other features.

The level of Pigsty integration differs between kernels. PostgreSQL, Citus, Babelfish, IvorySQL, PolarDB, AgensGraph, and pgEdge have defined templates and configuration procedures. Cloudberry and Greenplum usually use gpsql mode. For their MPP initialization and scale-out operations, upstream tools remain the preferred method.

item.title: Quick Start
item.description:
To use extensions in Pigsty, complete four steps: Download, Install, Config, and Create.

  1. Download: Download extension packages to the local repository. The default local repository only guarantees the base kernel and pgsql-main package set.
  2. Install: Install extension packages on cluster nodes
  3. Config: Some extensions need to be preloaded or configured with parameters
  4. Create: Execute CREATE EXTENSION in the database to create the extension

Declarative Configuration

Declare extensions in the Pigsty inventory. During cluster initialization, Pigsty installs their packages and creates the extensions automatically:

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Pigsty includes 600 precompiled PostgreSQL extensions that are ready to use.

What are Extensions

PostgreSQL extensions add database functionality without changes to the core code. An extension typically consists of three parts:

  • Control file (.control): Required, contains extension metadata
  • SQL scripts (.sql): Optional, defines functions, types, operators, and other database objects
  • Dynamic library (.so): Optional, provides high-performance functionality implemented in C

Extensions can add data types, index methods, functions, and operators to PostgreSQL. They can also add foreign data access, procedural languages, performance monitoring, security auditing, and other features.

item.title: Packages
item.description:
Pigsty uses package aliases to simplify extension installation and management.

Package Alias Mechanism

Extensions have different names at different layers:

Layer Example pgvector Example postgis
Extension Name vector postgis, postgis_topology, …
Package Alias pgvector postgis
RPM Package Name pgvector_18 postgis36_18*
DEB Package Name postgresql-18-pgvector postgresql-18-postgis-3*

Use a package alias to specify an extension without its RPM or DEB package name:

pg_extensions: [ pgvector, postgis, timescaledb ]  # Use package aliases

Pigsty converts each alias to the correct package names for the operating system and PostgreSQL version.

item.title: Download
item.description:
Before you install extensions, make sure that their packages are available from the local repository or an upstream repository.

Default Behavior

By default, Pigsty downloads the base PostgreSQL 18 kernel packages to the local software repository. The default extra download set is repo_extra_packages_default: [ pgsql-main ]. This set includes the PostgreSQL kernel, client, and procedural languages. It also includes basic extension packages such as pg_repack, wal2json, and pgvector.

item.title: Install
item.description:
Pigsty uses the operating system’s package manager (yum/apt) to install extension packages.

Related Parameters

Use these two parameters to specify which extensions to install:

Parameter Purpose Default Behavior
pg_packages Global common packages Ensure present (no upgrade)
pg_extensions Cluster-specific extensions Install latest version

Use pg_packages for essential extensions and base components that all clusters need. Typical components include the PostgreSQL kernel, Patroni, and pgBouncer.

Use pg_extensions for extensions that specific clusters need.

item.title: Config
item.description:
Some extensions require you to preload dynamic libraries or configure parameters before use. This section gives the configuration procedures.

Preload Extensions

After installation, you can enable most extensions with CREATE EXTENSION. Some extensions use PostgreSQL’s Hook mechanism and require preloading.

item.title: Update
item.description:
Update extensions at two levels: packages in the operating system, and extension objects in the database.

Update Packages

Use package managers to update extension packages:

# EL systems
sudo yum update pgvector_18*

# Debian/Ubuntu systems
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade postgresql-18-pgvector

Use Pigsty to update packages on multiple nodes:

# Update extension packages for specified cluster
./pgsql.yml -l pg-meta -t pg_extension -e '{"pg_extensions":["pgvector"]}'

# Using pig package manager
pig update pgvector

Update Extension Objects

After you update packages, you may also need to update the extension objects in the database.

item.title: Remove
item.description:
Extension removal has two levels: drop extension objects from the database, and uninstall packages from the operating system.

Drop Extension Objects

Use DROP EXTENSION to remove extensions from the database:

-- Drop extension
DROP EXTENSION pgvector;

-- If there are dependent objects, cascade delete is required
DROP EXTENSION pgvector CASCADE;

Warning: CASCADE will drop all objects that depend on this extension (tables, functions, views, etc.). Use with caution.

Why can’t my current user use the pg admin alias?

Since Pigsty v4.0, only members of admin on administration nodes can manage global Patroni and PostgreSQL clusters with pg.

The node.yml playbook creates the administration user dba with this permission. To grant the permission to your current user, explicitly add that user to the admin group:

item.title: Citus
item.description:
Pigsty natively supports Citus. This is a distributed horizontal scaling extension based on the native PostgreSQL kernel.

Installation

Citus is a PostgreSQL extension plugin. Use the standard extension installation procedure to install and enable it on a native PostgreSQL cluster.

./pgsql.yml -t pg_extension -e '{"pg_extensions":["citus"]}'

Configuration

To define a Citus cluster, set these parameters:

  • pg_mode must be set to citus instead of the default pgsql
  • You must define the shard name pg_shard and shard number pg_group on each shard cluster
  • You must define pg_primary_db to specify the database managed by Patroni
  • You can run administration commands as postgres from pg_dbsu, instead of the default pg_admin_username. If you use this account, you must set pg_dbsu_password to a non-empty plaintext password.

You also need HBA rules that allow SSL access from localhost and other data nodes.

item.title: IvorySQL
item.description:
IvorySQL is an open-source PostgreSQL kernel fork that aims to provide Oracle compatibility.

Overview

The Pigsty PGSQL repository provides IvorySQL 5.4 packages compatible with PostgreSQL 18.4. Packages cover the currently supported EL, Debian, and Ubuntu platforms on both architectures. Online installation uses Pigsty’s pgsql repository. The Professional Edition also provides offline delivery for these platforms.

Pigsty’s ivorysql package alias points to IvorySQL 5, which is compatible with PostgreSQL 18. Platform variables under roles/node_id/vars/ map the alias to package names. For example, EL uses ivorysql5, and Debian/Ubuntu uses ivorysql-5.

item.title: PolarDB PG
item.description:
Overview

Use Pigsty and PolarDB to create PostgreSQL clusters with “domestic innovation qualification” credentials.

PolarDB for PostgreSQL now uses PostgreSQL 17 as its base. The Pigsty polar template, default path, and extension notes now use PG17. Any client tool that supports the PostgreSQL wire protocol can connect to PolarDB clusters.

Pigsty’s PGSQL repository provides PolarDB PG open-source installation packages. Pigsty does not download these packages to the local software repository during installation.

item.title: PolarDB Oracle
item.description:
Use Pigsty to create PolarDB for Oracle clusters with “domestic innovation qualification” credentials.

The Security and Reliability Evaluation Results Announcement (No. 1, 2023) lists PolarDB v2.0 in Appendix 3, Centralized Database. It identifies PolarDB v2.0 as an autonomous, controllable, secure, and reliable domestic innovation database.

PolarDB for Oracle is an Oracle-compatible version based on PolarDB for PostgreSQL. Both use the same kernel. The --compatibility-mode parameter selects the mode.

item.title: Greenplum
item.description:
Pigsty supports deployment of Greenplum clusters and the derivative distribution YMatrixDB. You can also add existing Greenplum deployments to Pigsty monitoring.

Overview

Only the professional/enterprise editions provide Greenplum / YMatrix cluster deployment. This capability is not currently open source.

Installation
